source.title: Unstable Features, Reproducible Subspaces: Understanding Seed Dependence in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Gleb Gerasimov; T. Rusalev; Nikita Balagansky; Daniil Laptev; Vadim Kurochkin; Daniil Gavrilov

page_placements.theme: Cross-seed and cross-size reproducibility of SAE features

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies whether SAE features recur across random seeds and whether unstable features span reproducible subspaces. It mentions dictionary-size variation in related work but does not test feature splitting as dictionary size grows, or any of the listed split-specific versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's results concern cross-seed feature stability, feature subspaces, and related functional properties—not whether larger-dictionary features partition the inputs of smaller-dictionary features. The dictionary-size and feature-merging statement is attributed to prior work, so it is not recorded as a result of this study. The rows below record related findings that fit none of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures how often SAE features reappear across random seeds and the geometry of unstable features. It never tracks coarse features splitting into finer ones as dictionary size grows, and never tests absorption, hierarchy or larger-to-smaller latent decomposition. Feature splitting enters only through a related-work citation of Leask et al. (2025), that features vary with dictionary size and can be merged. The paper neither tests nor relies on the finding, so cites_only/T6 fits better than discusses.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that seed dependence is structured. Stable features carry most of the reconstruction and prediction signal; unstable ones are low-frequency surface-form triggers lying in reproducible lower-rank subspaces, reflecting basis ambiguity. They state this does not prove every unstable feature arises this way. Pooling high-probability cross-seed features yields more stable SAEs without losing explained variance, in that construction setting only.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures feature recurrence across random seeds and analyzes decoder subspaces; it does not use a dictionary-size sweep or test the coarse-to-fine input-partitioning procedure in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature endpoint membership and fractions depend on cosine threshold θ and endpoint cutoff ε; stability also varies across SAE family, sparsity setting, model, layer, and training budget.

fits_no_version.finding: GPT-2 layer 7 TopK SAEs (F=2^14, 96 seeds): mean reappearance p̂≈0.75; 8.0% of features unstable and 44.7% stable at ε=0.05, θ=0.7.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features split into a large cross-seed-stable subset and a smaller unstable subset.

fits_no_version.finding: Unstable decoder sets have lower effective rank than stable sets (ER/d 0.649 vs 0.808), and their top-r subspaces transfer across seeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Individually unstable SAE features can span reproducible lower-rank subspaces across seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: In a synthetic model, low-rank ground-truth features reappear across seeds with p≈0.25, while full-rank features are near-perfectly recovered.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low-rank shared structure is recoverable at the subspace level but not as individual SAE latents.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained on activations from a randomly initialized GPT-2 lose most of their stable features across θ values, unlike SAEs on trained GPT-2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-seed stability separates SAEs trained on trained versus random models.

record.problems: The paper does not test the claim's dictionary-size splitting behavior. It notes that the stable/unstable sets depend on cosine and endpoint thresholds, and says its low-rank analysis is evidence for a mechanism rather than proof that every unstable feature in real models has that cause. Some plotted results are described qualitatively without exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Other results on activation frequency, token entropy, automatic interpretations, feature-pool construction, masking effects on explained variance and next-token loss, SAE-family comparisons, training-token sweeps, and additional model/layer/dictionary-size configurations were not extracted: they concern stability or its consequences, not dictionary-size feature splitting. See Sections 5, 5.3, 7, Appendices B–E, and G.

untested.parts: No comparison of how features at one dictionary size map to finer features at a larger size. Table 6 varies F (2^14–2^16) but reports only cross-seed stable/unstable fractions.
Covers GPT-2, Pythia-160M and Gemma-2 2B with the authors' own SAEs, but only for seed stability, not splitting.
No nested feature families or concept hierarchy. The low-rank subspaces studied are cross-seed basis ambiguity, not parent/child families.
No parent/child firing or absorption measurement.
No test of larger-SAE latents decomposing into smaller-SAE latents, or of novel latents. Cross-seed non-identifiability is a different non-canonicity question.
Compares sparsity mechanisms (TopK, BatchTopK, JumpReLU, Vanilla, HierarchicalTopK) and Mahalanobis losses on seed stability only, not on splitting. No Matryoshka SAE.

record.verdict_notes: r9 and r10 describe the same Figure 8 contrast from two sides; this is redundant but harmless. The main-setting unstable/stable fractions differ between tables: Table 6 gives 0.080/0.447 for GPT-2 L7 F=2^14, while Table 1 gives 0.098/0.522 for TopK k=64 in nominally the same setting. The paper does not explain the difference; possibly the number of seeds differs. The dictionary-size columns of Table 6 show stability changing with F, not splitting, so they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare increasing dictionary sizes or test whether finer features cover the inputs of a coarse feature and lie near its direction.
Does not test whether dictionary-size feature splitting holds in large models or open SAE releases.
Does not test nested split-feature families or whether they mirror a hierarchy of concepts.
Does not test parent-child activation partitioning or whether size or sparsity changes fix absorption.
Does not test whether larger-SAE latents decompose into smaller-SAE latents or whether larger SAEs add novel latents.

Although it compares SAE variants and sparsity settings, it does not test whether splitting is caused by the SAE objective on correlated or hierarchical inputs, or whether Matryoshka SAEs change splitting.

relation.reason: The text never discusses feature splitting. Its only claim-related content is one related-work sentence on Leask et al. (2025), saying features vary with dictionary size and can be merged. Bricken et al. 2023 is cited only as a generic SAE reference.

tranche.reason: The study measures cross-seed feature recurrence and decoder-subspace geometry. It never tracks coarse features splitting into finer ones as dictionary size grows, and it tests no version.

source_check.notes: This is a seed-stability study of SAE features and has no feature-splitting measurement. For the nominal main setting (GPT-2 L7, TopK 64, F=2^14), the paper reports different endpoint fractions in different places: Table 6 gives 0.080/0.447 (seed count unstated), Table 1 gives 0.098/0.522, and Figs 7/22 give 0.0786/0.611 at 10B tokens.

statements.problem: Numbers match: mean p-hat ≈ 0.75 (Fig. 1: 0.7460), unstable 0.080 and stable 0.447 (Table 6, GPT-2 L7, F=2^14), ER/d 0.649 vs 0.808 (Table 5). Cross-seed subspace transfer is in Fig. 5 / Sec. 6.2. Caveat: Table 6 does not state its seed count, and Table 1 gives 0.098/0.522 for TopK k=64 in the same nominal setting.
